activities.anchor: a trade, not a tournament with a single winner
activities.caption: true or false — two strategies, one goal
activities.name: rpStrategyJudge

statements.s: An asexual lineage doubles its numbers every generation and never needs a partner.
statements.why: Fast, cheap and safe when the environment suits you — which is why bacteria and many plants still run it.

statements.s: Asexual reproduction is a primitive mistake that evolution abandoned.
statements.why: Anything but — it is a running strategy, not a relic.

statements.s: Sex persists despite its cost because variation is insurance against fast-evolving parasites.
statements.why: A sexual lineage spends half its reproduction making offspring that carry only half of each parent's genes.

statements.s: Sexual reproduction is always the better strategy in every environment.
statements.why: It is a trade, not a tournament — the payoff shows only across generations under attack from evolving parasites.

activities.caption: pair each structure with its engineering job
activities.name: rpGameteMatch

config.prompt: Two gametes, built differently — pair each structure with its job:

pairs.right: changes at fertilisation to lock out competitors
the egg's opposite bet — stocked, immobile, defended

config.why: Sperm are cheap and expendable by design; eggs are precious — an asymmetry repeated across nearly all animal species, shaping mating behaviour everywhere.

activities.anchor: about 1,500 per second in a healthy male
activities.caption: call the magnitude — the sperm production line
activities.name: rpSpermEstimate

config.prompt: Sperm are made continuously from puberty onward. Roughly how many does a healthy male produce per second?
config.why: About 1,500 per second — and yet only a few hundred of a typical ejaculate's 40–300 million survive the journey far enough to reach the egg.
config.context: Eggs are the opposite: all the precursor cells exist before birth, and one follicle matures per month.

activities.anchor: because a polyspermic zygote cannot develop
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the fertilisation relay
activities.name: rpPolySpot

config.prompt: This fertilisation answer contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: Millions of sperm are deposited; only a few hundred survive the journey far enough to reach the egg.
Acrosome enzymes digest a path through the jelly coat.
The moment one sperm gets through, the egg membrane changes — no second sperm may enter.
A polyspermic zygote would develop normally, just smaller.
Nuclei fuse: 23 + 23 chromosomes restore the diploid 46.
config.correction: A polyspermic zygote CANNOT develop — the hardening of the coat is exactly what prevents it.
config.why: Fertilisation is a gate, not a finish line: millions of candidates filtered, then the door locked behind the one.

activities.caption: file the claims — crosses the placenta or not
activities.name: rpPlacentaBuckets

config.prompt: The placenta is the only exchange site. File each claim:

items.label: dissolved nutrients and oxygen — mother to fetus
urea and carbon dioxide — fetus to mother
alcohol, nicotine, rubella and HIV — the warning list
about 25 mL of oxygen per minute at full term
the mother's blood mixing with the fetus's
the fetus breathing through the umbilical cord

config.why: The two bloods stay separate while substances diffuse across — the cord is plumbing between fetus and placenta, and the fetal lungs are collapsed and bypassed by a shunt until the first breaths.

config.prompt: From maturing follicle to shed lining — put the cycle in order:
items: FSH from the pituitary matures a follicle
The follicle's oestrogen rebuilds the uterine lining
Oestrogen rising high enough triggers the LH surge — the one positive feedback in endocrinology
Ovulation, about day 14 in a 28-day cycle
The emptied follicle becomes the corpus luteum, secreting progesterone
If no embryo signals, progesterone collapses and the lining is shed
config.why: One positive and one negative feedback loop in the same cycle: oestrogen's rise triggers LH, while progesterone suppresses further FSH.

activities.anchor: lets cycle-tracking apps guess your ovulation day
activities.caption: pin the post-ovulatory plateau on the thermometer
activities.name: rpBBTPlace

config.prompt: Progesterone raises basal body temperature by 0.3–0.5 °C after ovulation. If the pre-ovulatory reading sits near 36.4 °C, pin the post-ovulatory plateau (°C):
config.why: About 36.8 °C — a fraction of a degree, held until menstruation; the signal is small, which is why tracking demands a good thermometer and daily patience.
config.context: The step is progesterone's signature — the corpus luteum warming the body after ovulation.

activities.anchor: The same hormone logic powers both
activities.caption: press the switches — contraception or IVF
activities.name: rpTechBranch

config.root: The menstrual cycle's feedback loop can be pressed deliberately — in either direction. Choose the goal.

choices.label: No follicle matures this month
choices.feedback: The combined pill supplies oestrogen and progesterone at steady levels — the cycle's own negative-feedback switch, held on.

choices.label: Several follicles mature at once
choices.feedback: IVF runs the loop in reverse: fertility drugs push the follicle-stimulating switch hard.

choices.label: Delay or prevent ovulation after the fact
choices.feedback: The morning-after pill loads progesterone high enough to delay ovulation.

choices.label: A purely mechanical barrier
choices.feedback: Condoms — and, uniquely among contraceptives, they also block STI transmission.

pill.text: The switch pressed and held: no egg released, nothing to fertilise.

ivf.text: Eggs collected, fertilised in a dish, and one or two embryos placed back into a progesterone-primed uterus.

morning.text: A progesterone surge buying time — the corpus luteum's own chemistry, borrowed.

condom.text: The one technology that needs no hormone at all.

config.why: Both hormonal technologies press the cycle's own feedback switches in opposite directions — STIs, by contrast, are defined by transmission route, not species.
